content: Sinus arrhythmia is characterized by a P-P interval of 160 milliseconds or more in the presence of normal P waves. It is the most common type of arrhythmia and is primarily classified into respiratory sinus arrhythmia and non-respiratory sinus arrhythmia. Respiratory sinus arrhythmia is a normal physiological variant that is most commonly observed in younger individuals and tends to diminish with age. In contrast, non-respiratory sinus arrhythmia is more frequently seen in elderly individuals, particularly those with underlying heart disease. Sinus arrhythmia is often associated with slower heart rates or occurs following an increase in vagal tone. It typically resolves as the heart rate increases. Triggers for sinus arrhythmia include sinoatrial block, sinus pause, premature atrial beats, carotid massage, and the use of parasympathomimetic medications. Classification Respiratory Sinus Arrhythmia Respiratory sinus arrhythmia is linked to variations in heart rate that correspond to the respiratory cycle. These changes are secondary to fluctuations in vagal tone, with heart rate increasing during inspiration and decreasing during expiration. This type of sinus arrhythmia is considered a normal variant and is most commonly observed in young individuals. Non-Respiratory Sinus Arrhythmia In non-respiratory sinus arrhythmia, the variation in the P-P interval is not related to the respiratory cycle. While it can occur in individuals with normal hearts, it is more commonly observed in elderly patients with heart disease. The underlying cause of non-respiratory sinus arrhythmia is often unknown, but known causes include: Side effects of medications such as digitalis or morphine Elevated intracranial pressure Inferior myocardial infarction Recovery from certain illnesses Ventriculophasic Sinus Arrhythmia Ventriculophasic sinus arrhythmia is most frequently observed in patients with partial or complete atrioventricular (AV) block. It can also occur following a compensatory pause induced by a premature ventricular contraction. In this condition, the P-P interval that does not contain a QRS complex is longer than the P-P interval that does contain a QRS complex.
